title: Indian-Origin Woman Arrested in Canada for Allegedly Defrauding Renters of Over $60,000
excerpt: Canadian police say the suspect collected deposits and rent payments for properties she did not own, leaving multiple victims without housing or their money.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • An Indian-origin woman was arrested in Canada for defrauding renters of over $60,000.
  • The suspect collected deposits for properties she did not own or have authority to rent.
  • Victims included new immigrants and students, exacerbating their housing struggles.
  • Police encourage other potential victims to report similar fraud cases.

Canadian police have arrested an Indian-origin woman for allegedly running a rental fraud scheme that defrauded multiple tenants of more than $60,000. The suspect reportedly collected security deposits and rent payments for properties she neither owned nor had authorization to rent, leaving victims — many of them recent immigrants — without housing or their money.

The Scheme

According to police, the accused advertised rental properties on popular listing platforms, conducted viewings, collected deposits and first-month rent payments, and provided fake lease agreements. Victims only discovered the fraud when they showed up to move in and found the properties occupied by actual tenants or locked with no access.

The losses, exceeding $60,000 across multiple victims, represent devastating blows for people who were already stretching limited budgets to secure housing in one of the most expensive rental markets in North America.

A Crisis Exploited

Canada's housing crisis has created fertile ground for rental scams. With vacancy rates near historic lows in major cities like Toronto, Vancouver, and Calgary, desperate renters — particularly new immigrants and international students — are vulnerable to schemes that exploit their urgency and unfamiliarity with local norms.

Language barriers, the pressure to secure housing before arriving in Canada, and willingness to send money sight-unseen have made immigrant communities particularly susceptible. Many victims are reluctant to report fraud due to embarrassment or concerns about their immigration status.

Protecting Yourself

Police have urged potential victims of the accused to come forward. For those navigating Canada's rental market, experts recommend never sending money before independently verifying the landlord's ownership through property records, insisting on in-person viewings, using only established platforms with built-in protections, and never paying in cash or via untraceable transfers.

The case serves as a painful reminder that in a housing market defined by scarcity and desperation, those with the least familiarity with the system often bear the greatest risk.
